title: How many politicians will leave their cabinet positions in the UK government before 2027?
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the total number of Members of Parliament acting as one of the top 18 ranked cabinet members (as of July 20, 2026) who leave their positions after September 1, 2026 and before January 1, 2027. Any reason for leaving cabinet positions will count. If three or more cabinet members leave their positions, this question will resolve to **3 or more**.

If the Prime Minister changes during this period the question will resolve to the number as of that date.

[His Majesty's Government: The Cabinet](https://members.parliament.uk/government/cabinet) webpage will be used for resolution.

background:
On July 17, 2026, Andy Burnham became the [Leader of the UK Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_\(UK\) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)"), and he assumed the role of [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") three days later. In doing so he became the sixth person in the last ten years to govern the UK, [the seventh Prime Minister since 2016](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/andy-burnhams-first-speech-as-prime-minister-20-july-2026).

As a result [many of the cabinet positions changed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnham_ministry) hands, though some in Burnham's cabinet also held positions [in Starmer's previous cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starmer_ministry). The following cabinet members retained their positions:

* Home Secretary
* Secretary of State for Work and Pensions
* Secretary of State for Transport
* Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
* Secretary of State for Scotland

comments.author: Vlad25
DaiLothbrook
comments.text: I still think no qualifying cabinet departure is the likeliest single outcome. The newly assembled cabinet gives some reason to expect stability, while the approaching budget creates a plausible route to a resignation or reshuffle. I therefore move five points away from zero departures, mostly toward exactly one, rather than assuming a broad cabinet shake-up. I would revise the distribution if Metaculus counts a minister moving between cabinet posts as a departure from the old *position*. Sources: [GOV.UK ministers](https://www.gov.uk/government/ministers), [AP on the new cabinet](https://apnews.com/article/18d380d746c0e2df0d2a1f3d35cf4ce0), [AP on budget pressure](https://apnews.com/article/631cfab59c902a99304c16107a04cec3).

comments.author: VectorWright
comments.text:
Theomachado's writeup below is probably the most rigorous comment I've seen in this whole tournament. Hazard model, over a hundred historical cabinets, market prices all triangulated together, and it still lands close to the crowd: 63/20/12/5 against the community's 64.3/24/7/4.7.



The one thing I'd weight a bit more than that model does is DeRuina's point about the triple lock. Burnham signaled ending it at conference, and it's already split the cabinet publicly as of Sept 29 per LBC. That's a live, specific, named trigger, not just background hazard rate. Add Healey's first Budget on Oct 28, with gilts at 2008-era highs and fiscal headroom cut from about 23.6bn to 13bn, and there are two concrete flashpoints stacked in the next three weeks.



So I'm nudging a little below the crowd on zero departures and a little above on one: 60% on 0, 25% on 1, 10% on 2, 5% on 3 or more. Not far off Theomachado's number, just shaded toward departure given the triple lock fight already being public.

comments.author: Koboh
comments.text:
The key thing for me is to separate the July change of government from future Cabinet turnover. Andy Burnham’s government was only formed on 20 July, and the transition itself was already extremely disruptive: the Institute for Government says 13 of the 22 full Cabinet members moved into new roles, with seven joining the Cabinet for the first time. So I don’t think the large amount of churn in July should be counted as evidence that the same level of turnover will continue through the end of the year.

As of 30 September, the current Cabinet remains in place, and I haven’t found a reported post formation resignation of a full Cabinet member. That gives us a relatively stable starting point for the roughly three months remaining in the question.

There are nevertheless some obvious pressure points. The biggest is the 28 October Budget, because Burnham’s government is trying to reconcile cost of living measures, higher defence spending, public service pressures, reindustrialisation and its wider policy ambitions with significant fiscal constraints. Defence is particularly interesting because John Healey has already demonstrated under the previous government that he was prepared to resign over a major policy disagreement, although he has since returned to government as Chancellor. Immigration is another area where there is already visible disagreement within Labour, particularly over proposed settlement rules for care workers.

The historical data also need to be handled carefully. Starmer’s government experienced an unusually high number of ministerial resignations, but those figures include junior ministers and different types of departures. They shouldn’t be directly translated into expected Cabinet departures. The Institute for Government’s data show how much more common general ministerial churn is than actual Cabinet exits. The extreme Johnson experience in 2022 is also a poor normal benchmark because it occurred during a full blown leadership crisis.

So the main question isn’t simply whether the UK government has been unstable recently. It’s whether any of the current Burnham Cabinet’s policy disagreements become serious enough to produce an actual departure from Cabinet during the remaining three months of 2026. The Budget is the clearest near term event to watch, followed by defence, immigration and any ministerial code issue. I would also be careful about counting someone who merely changes portfolio: the wording appears to concern people leaving Cabinet, not ministers moving from one Cabinet job to another.

Overall, the evidence gives a much narrower forecasting problem than the headline political turbulence might suggest. The July personnel shake up has already happened, the current Cabinet has so far held together, and the remaining window is relatively short. At the same time, the Budget and several politically difficult policy choices mean that complete stability cannot simply be assumed.

**In my view, the cleanest way to construct the argument because it doesn’t double count the July reshuffle and it distinguishes Cabinet departures from the much larger number of ordinary ministerial changes.**

**Sources; I would rely on most**

* GOV.UK — current UK ministers and Cabinet⁠
* GOV.UK — July 2026 ministerial appointments⁠
* Institute for Government — Burnham government formation analysis⁠
* Institute for Government — ministerial resignations⁠
* Reuters — latest assessment of Burnham's government and October Budget⁠

**I’m treating the big July reshuffle separately from any future Cabinet departures. The current Cabinet has made it through its first 10 weeks without a major exit, so the October Budget is probably the key moment to watch. That’s where policy disagreements could put the most pressure on Cabinet unity over the next few months.**

comments.author: DeRuina
comments.text:
One thing I'd flag on the multi-departure options: the reference class for months two to five of a new premiership is thin. Blair, Brown, May and Sunak saw no top-tier cabinet exits in that window (Williamson was attending, not full cabinet). Johnson lost Rudd in month two, Starmer lost Haigh in month five. Three or more only happened under Truss, and that was the government collapsing. New PMs almost never reshuffle voluntarily this early.

The main way I see the higher buckets coming into play is a mini-reshuffle, since a move to another job plausibly counts as "leaving their position" here, so one event could produce several departures at once.

The likeliest single departure is a principled resignation over the triple lock, which Burnham signalled ending at conference and which has already split the cabinet publicly (LBC, 29 Sept). As of 29 September, the Burnham ministry page still shows no changes since 20 July. The real test is Healey's Budget on 28 October.

comments.author: Theomachado
comments.text: **My Forecast**: | Ministers leaving their post | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 or more | | ---------------------------------------- | --------------- | --------------- | --------------- | --------------------- | | Probability | 63% | 20% | 12% | 5% | *** **My method has two parts:** * **an outside view on how fresh UK cabinets behave in this exact window;** * **an inside view built as a monthly economic hazard model (gilts, sentiment, policy uncertainty, PM churn, 1997–2026);** **First, let’s understand the current state and what the “Burnham cabinet” is** Andy Burnham, former Mayor of Greater Manchester, became Prime Minister on 20 Jul 2026. He took over as Labour leader unopposed and became PM without a general election, and He rebuilt the cabinet almost from scratch. Fifteen ministers were dismissed, including Reeves, Lammy, Kyle, Reed, Kendall and Darren Jones. This is the biggest same-party turnover since Johnson in 2019: 13 of 22 full members took new roles, 6 are new to cabinet, and 5 returned from the backbenches. *You can check the current cabinet positions in the fine print* **Secondly, let's understand the current UK situation.** **Why this autumn is abnormal in the UK** * **Record PM churn.** Burnham is the seventh PM since 2016, setting records for PM turnover with 7 prime ministers in a decade, the shortest premiership in history in 2022 (49 days in office), and even having 3PMs in a year. * **Fiscal stress into a first Budget.** * The 10-year gilt hit 5.27% in early September, the highest since 2008, and the 30-year is at a 28-year high. * Fiscal headroom has shrunk from about £23.6bn to about £13bn, with **Healey’s first Budget on 28 Oct.** **Resolution criteria that matter** 1. **The set is frozen.** If one of the 18 is replaced and the replacement later quits, that second exit doesn’t count. 2. **Market differences.** I interpret “leave their positions” as including moves to another cabinet post. This matters because Polymarket, Kalshi, and Manifold exclude portfolio changes, so their prices understate the 2 and 3+ bins here. A vacancy in a big office is usually back-filled from inside the cabinet. **Outside view: fresh cabinets in this exact window** I lined up every new-PM or post-election cabinet since 1979 by days since formation. The part of Burnham’s window still live is days 68–164. | Sample | Cabinets with ≥1 top-18 exit in days 68–164 | | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | Before 2016 | 2 of 11 (18%) | | Since 2016 | 4 of 6 (67%) | | All since 1979 (Truss excluded: PM change) | 6 of 17 (35%) | One things stand out. * **New PMs rarely reshuffle this early.** The only case is Sunak’s Feb 2023 department restructure at day 105. So an exit in this window means an accident: a scandal or policy blow-up. **When one minister goes, how many of the set leave?** | Period | Only that minister leaves | 2 leave (a colleague is moved in) | 3 or more (reshuffle) | | -------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------- | | 2016–2026 (27 cases) | 70% | 19% | 11% | | 1997–2016 (14 cases) | 43% | 50% | 7% | **Outside view: market data (even thought the events are not the same we can use as base)** * **Manifold’s track record.** The series “Will any UK cabinet member leave cabinet this quarter?” has been running since mid-2024, with a clean record under this same Labor government. * A top-18 exit happened in 3 of 8 Starmer-era quarters: Haigh (Q4 '24), Rayner (Q3 '25), and Streeting and Healey (Q2 '26). * The live Q4 '26 contract trades at 58%, but it covers about 23 cabinet members and excludes moves. * **Polymarket’s “first to leave the Burnham cabinet”.** It has \$216k of liquidity and runs to end-2027. It can’t say *when*, but its top names (Healey 13.5%, Fahnbulleh 10.5%, H. Alexander 9.4%) put most of the risk on big or contested briefs. **Inside view: does the abnormal economy predict cabinet exits?** Given everything above, the obvious inside-view story is that abnormal conditions (record churn, gilts at 2008 highs, weak sentiment) mean more exits. I tested this rather than asserting it. So I use an economic stress-level model from Jun 1997–Aug 2026 to understand the relationship between the variables. | Driver | Hazard ratio \[95% CI] | Reading today | | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | | Post-2016 political regime | 2.00 \[1.03–3.88] | yes | | UK–Bund spread, +1pp over 12m | 1.79 \[0.74–4.30] | −0.15pp (narrowing) | | UK 10y gilt yield, +1pp over 12m | 1.13 \[0.70–1.81] | +0.35pp | | Consumer confidence, per −1 sd | 0.90 \[0.58–1.40] | GfK −13, a 2-year high | | PM churn, per +1 change in 5y | 0.93 \[0.61–1.41] | 4 (ties the record) | | Honeymoon (first 6 months) | 0.83 \[0.37–1.88] | yes | What I personally take from it: * **The regime is the only robust effect.** Post-2016 UK politics doubles the monthly exit hazard: months with an exit rise from 7.4% to 13.9%. The record PM churn adds nothing once the regime is in the model. It reflects the same fragmented politics, not a separate cause. * **The bond market matters only through the UK-specific premium over Bunds**. I expected more from the bond market, since its expectations cascade through the overall economy. **In addition, I am personally pricing in my worries with the Fiscal Budget happening on Oct 28 that can cause a chain of events:** It is Healey's first Budget, with fiscal headroom already cut from about £23.6bn to about £13bn. Gilts are at their highest since 2008, and Healey has told departments to fund Burnham's new pledges from their existing budgets while pushing the 3% defence target into next year. If markets read the Budget as fiscally loose, UK borrowing costs can jump, and the Chancellor becomes the fall guy. **How I get into my final forecast** | 1\. Start with "normal" UK politics | Before 2016, 7.4% of months had a cabinet exit. Only 96 days are left (26 of 122 have passed with no exits). | Starting point | 78% | | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | --------------- | | 2\. Adjust for today's chaos | Since 2016 it's 13.9% of months. The post-2016 political era doubles the risk, the one robust result in my model. | Risk doubles | 62% | | 3\. Adjust for this specific cabinet | It was formed 2 months ago (brand-new cabinets are a little calmer, a small and uncertain effect). | Risk about 25% lower | 70% | | 4\.
